opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's one of the questions I find most interesting, and I don't think we've fully solved it yet.

The way I think about it is in terms of the brain, and the idea that memory consolidation happens at different timescales. Some parts of your memory adapt very quickly to whatever is in front of you right now. Other parts change slowly and hold more persistent, abstract knowledge. In the continuum memory view, each MLP block is a memory with its own update frequency. The fast ones are closer to the context, and the slow ones are closer to what we'd traditionally call pre-trained weights.

The question is how information should flow between those levels. The simplest version, which is roughly what we did initially, is a sequential chain. The input goes through the blocks in order, and each block is optimized at its own rate. The higher-frequency block compresses the recent context, and its output becomes the input to the slower block. So knowledge transfers implicitly through the forward pass. The slow block sees a summary of what the fast block has learned, aggregated over a longer window, and it updates less often. That loosely resembles systems consolidation, where something learned quickly gets gradually written into longer-term storage.

But that's only one design choice, and I think there are several others worth exploring.

One is initialization. When a fast block resets or starts a new chunk, it could be initialized from the slower block, or meta-learned by it. Then the slow memory acts like a prior, and the fast memory adapts on top of it. That's very much the nested learning view: the outer, slower level learns how the inner, faster level should start and learn.

Another is the reverse direction, where the slow block's update is partly driven by what the fast blocks found surprising. You don't want to consolidate everything; you want to move the things that were important or recurring. So you can think of a gating or selection mechanism that decides what is worth transferring from short-term to long-term.

There's also the parallel option. Instead of a chain, all the blocks see the same input, each updating at its own frequency, and you aggregate their outputs. That gives you more of a mixture of timescales than a hierarchy. It's a different inductive bias, and which one works better probably depends on the task.

The part I care about most is forgetting. If transfer goes in only one direction and the slow memory just accumulates, you lose plasticity. If the fast memory overwrites too aggressively, you get catastrophic forgetting. The point of having a spectrum of frequencies is that something forgotten at one level can still survive at another, and ideally can be recovered through the connections between levels. So I'd say transfer should be bidirectional, selective, and matched to the timescale of each level, rather than just stacking blocks and hoping it works.

We're still early, honestly. I think there's a lot of room for people to design better consolidation mechanisms here, and that's where many of the gains in continual learning are going to come from.

r001.rationale: The response describes the fast block passing a compressed context summary to the slower block, but does not say this transfer happens before updating the fast block.

r002.rationale: It describes the fast block compressing recent context and feeding that summary to the slower block, explicitly presenting this as implicit knowledge transfer between blocks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the core design question in nested learning, and I think the honest answer is that we don't fully know yet, but we have some strong intuitions from how the brain does it.

So the way I think about it is, when you have a level that updates very frequently, say every token or every few tokens, that level is essentially acting as working memory. It's capturing the context of the current sequence, the current document, whatever the immediate input is. And then you have slower levels that update maybe every chunk, or every thousand tokens, or in the extreme case, only during pretraining, which is the standard transformer MLP. Those slower levels are supposed to hold more abstract, more consolidated knowledge.

And the question of transfer is really: how does information flow from the fast level into the slow level, and how does the slow level inform what the fast level is doing?

I think the cleanest way to frame it is as a consolidation process. In the brain, you have the hippocampus doing rapid encoding, and then during sleep or during offline periods, that information gets replayed and gradually written into the neocortex, which learns much more slowly. The slow system doesn't memorize everything the fast system saw. It extracts the statistical regularities, the things that keep showing up across many episodes.

So in our framework, the natural analog is that the slow level's update should be a function of what the fast level has accumulated. You can think of the fast level's parameters, or its state, as a compressed summary of recent context, and the slow level takes a gradient step based on that summary rather than on raw tokens. That gives you a kind of hierarchical compression where each level sees a more abstracted view of the data than the level below it.

The other direction, slow informing fast, is actually simpler in some sense. The slow level provides the initialization or the prior for the fast level. So when the fast memory resets or decays, it doesn't start from nothing. It starts from whatever the slow level has learned is a good default. In the Titans line of work, this showed up as the deep memory module being conditioned on, or being initialized from, parameters that were learned during pretraining. And in nested learning we try to make that recursive, so each level is the prior for the level above it in frequency.

There are a couple of things I want to flag as open. One is the question of what the update rule itself should be. If every level is just doing gradient descent on some surprise metric, you have to decide whether the surprise is computed with respect to the raw input or with respect to the fast level's prediction error. I lean toward the latter. The slow level should only learn things the fast level couldn't handle on its own, otherwise you get redundancy and the levels collapse into doing the same thing.

The second open issue is the frequency ratio. If the slow level updates too rarely, it never sees enough of the fast level's evolution to extract anything meaningful. If it updates too often, it's just another fast level and you've lost the abstraction hierarchy. We've mostly set these ratios by hand, and I think the right answer eventually is that the frequencies themselves should be learned, maybe gated by how much the lower level's state has drifted.

And then there's the forgetting side, which people underrate. Transfer isn't just about writing knowledge up the hierarchy. The fast level has to be able to let go of things once they've been consolidated, otherwise its capacity fills up with stuff that's already been stored somewhere more permanent. So I'd argue the transfer mechanism and the forgetting mechanism have to be designed together. You consolidate and then you release.

So to put it simply: fast levels compress context, slow levels compress fast levels, slow levels initialize fast levels, and the whole thing works only if each level learns what the level below it failed to capture. That's the picture I have in my head, and most of the design decisions in the architecture fall out of trying to make that picture concrete.

r001.rationale: The response describes the slower level learning from a summary of the faster level, but does not say this transfer happens before updating the faster block.

r002.rationale: It proposes that the slower level update from a compressed summary of the fast level’s accumulated context rather than raw tokens, which is a semantic description of context distillation.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that these blocks operate at different timescales, so knowledge transfer should happen at different timescales too. A block that updates frequently can adapt to the current context very quickly. But you don’t necessarily want every change in that block to immediately propagate into a slower block, because then you lose the benefit of having a slower, more stable memory.

So the question becomes: what is worth consolidating? If something keeps being useful across contexts, that’s a signal that it should influence the slower-updating blocks. And the transfer should go both ways. The slower blocks provide a stable foundation that the faster blocks can use while adapting to new information.

Importantly, I wouldn’t think of this as simply copying weights between MLPs. They may represent information differently. What you want to transfer is useful behavior or predictive information, through an objective that connects them. The design challenge is to allow that communication while preserving the different timescales; otherwise, you effectively end up with one memory system updating at the same rate.

r001.rationale: It says useful changes in fast blocks should influence slower blocks, but does not specify transferring them before the faster block updates.

r002.rationale: It proposes an objective connecting the blocks, but does not identify context distillation as the transfer method.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that knowledge transfer should happen on the timescale of the block that’s receiving it. If you have an MLP that updates frequently, it can absorb information from the current context very quickly. But you don’t necessarily want every one of those updates to immediately change a slower MLP, because then you lose the benefit of having different frequencies in the first place.

So the faster block can accumulate information, and when the slower block updates, there’s an opportunity to consolidate what has been useful across those interactions. And the transfer can go the other way as well: the slower block provides a more stable representation that helps guide the faster adaptation.

The important question is what gets transferred. You don’t necessarily want to copy parameters between blocks. You want a learning signal that lets each block incorporate useful information into its own representation. That way, you have both rapid adaptation and something more persistent, without forcing the whole system to operate at one timescale.

r001.rationale: The response says the faster block can accumulate information and the slower block can consolidate it when it updates, but it does not specify transferring knowledge before updating the faster block.

r002.rationale: The response describes transferring a learning signal, but does not identify context distillation as the method.
